unit.name: Around the World in 80 Days by Verne / Eason
unit.subtitle: Phileas Fogg's Victorian wager turned into a high-speed feat of multi-roling and ensemble theatre.

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students retell what happened in the production scene by scene rather than analysing how meaning was communicated through specific performer or design choices and why those choices worked for the audience.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 teacher resources, Live Theatre guidance — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/subject-content/understanding-drama

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students answer set-play questions as essay-style literary analysis rather than as a performer or designer making concrete physical, vocal, lighting, sound, set or costume choices for a specific moment.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 specification, Section B requirements — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/scheme-of-assessment

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe design ideas in general terms (a dark mood, period costume) rather than naming specific elements such as lantern type, gobo, fabric, colour, fitting and the meaning each generates.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 mark scheme conventions and theatrical skills guidance — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/subject-content/guidance-on-theatrical-skills

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students write 'I would say it angrily' without specifying volume, pace, pitch, pause, gesture, posture, facial expression or proxemics for the named moment.
common_misconceptions.source: AQA GCSE Drama 8261 specification, performer skills — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/subject-content/guidance-on-theatrical-skills

common_misconceptions.misconception: Students describe a practitioner's biography but do not apply the techniques to a specific moment of the set play or live production.
common_misconceptions.source: Britannica entry on Brecht and the alienation effect — britannica.com/art/alienation-effect; Britannica entry on epic theatre — britannica.com/art/epic-theatre

student_errors_by_question_type.4 marks — Explain Effect: Students name a design element but do not explain its effect on the audience or its link to character, theme or context.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Interpret as Performer: Students describe what their character is feeling without translating it into specific vocal and physical choices anchored to a named moment of the play.
student_errors_by_question_type.8 marks — Interpret as Designer: Students give one design idea per skill (lighting, sound, set, costume) but do not justify the choice with reference to the moment's meaning or the designer's intention.
student_errors_by_question_type.12 marks — Analyse Intentions: Students describe events in the play instead of analysing what the playwright is trying to make the audience think, feel or understand at that moment.
student_errors_by_question_type.20 marks — Extended Staging Response: Students drift off the named focus of the question and write a general staging answer; they also under-use the extract, treating it as a prompt rather than reading specific lines and stage directions.
student_errors_by_question_type.32 marks — Live Theatre Review: Students retell plot rather than evaluating specific performer or design choices, and they fail to make a justified judgement about how successfully meaning was communicated to the audience.

topic_weighting_notes: The set-play section (Section B equivalent) carries 44 of 80 marks on the written paper — set-play units must be the most detailed and most rehearsed in the curriculum. Source: aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/specification-at-a-glance

The live theatre review carries 32 of 80 marks. Treat Unit 3 as a generic-skills unit because each student writes about a production they have personally seen, not a prescribed text. Source: aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/scheme-of-assessment

Theatre roles and stagecraft (Section A equivalent) carries only 4 of 80 marks but underpins every other answer because students must use the correct stagecraft vocabulary throughout. Source: aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification/specification-at-a-glance
current_spec_changes: Specification version 1.7 (26 April 2022) is current; the nine prescribed plays remain unchanged. Source: specs/aqa/drama-8261-8261.md frontmatter and AQA specification page — aqa.org.uk/subjects/drama/gcse/drama-8261/specification

From 2019 onwards students must experience at least one live performance; digital streamings are no longer sufficient as the only experience. Source: AQA specification 8261, Area of study 2 — Live theatre production
pedagogical_notes: Drama benefits from regular, low-stakes retrieval of stagecraft vocabulary and practitioner techniques. Build retrieval activities into every set-play lesson and every revision technique guide. Source: Education Endowment Foundation Arts Participation summary — educationendowmentfoundation.org.uk/education-evidence/teaching-learning-toolkit/arts-participation

Pair text-based study with brief practical activity (read a moment, stand it up, discuss the choices) — practical engagement raises attainment in extended-response writing about the same moment. Source: National Theatre Learn — nationaltheatre.org.uk/learn-explore/schools/teacher-resources/

For live theatre review, teach a What/How/Why scaffolding so students always describe the choice, explain how it created meaning and judge why it worked or did not. Source: National Theatre teacher resources for GCSE Drama — nationaltheatre.org.uk/learn-explore/schools/teacher-resources/gcse-drama-resources-for-set-texts/

drama_content_rules.perform_or_design_lens: Every set-play lesson must teach students to think as performer AND as designer for at least one named moment. Worked examples and exam-tip blocks must include both vocal/physical choices and at least one design discipline (lighting, sound, set or costume).
drama_content_rules.stage_terminology_required: Every set-play lesson should use and gloss stage-craft terms: stage left/right, upstage/downstage, blocking, proxemics, levels, focus, gestus, tableau, naturalistic vs stylised, lighting state/wash/special/gobo, sound cue, costume choice for character, set design, props as symbols.
drama_content_rules.no_plot_reproduction: Lessons must NEVER paraphrase the plot scene-by-scene or quote more than 15 words from any in-copyright play. Reference moments by name only (e.g. 'the moment Mickey learns the truth in Blood Brothers' or 'the linen scene in The Crucible') without reproducing dialogue.
drama_content_rules.quotation_cap_strict: Maximum 15 words from any in-copyright play, maximum once per lesson, in quotation marks. Better: paraphrase the situation. Public-domain Shakespeare (Romeo and Juliet) may be quoted more freely but still keep quotes short and purposeful.
drama_content_rules.practice_question_stems: Practice question stems must ask about staging, performance or design moments without reproducing the playwright's text. GOOD: 'How might a director use lighting to emphasise the shift in mood when Mickey learns the truth in Blood Brothers?' BAD: 'Mickey says "[long quote]". How does the writer...'
drama_content_rules.live_theatre_review_unit_only_generic: Unit 3 'Live Theatre Review' must teach generic skills only. Worked examples must use FICTIONAL productions (e.g. 'imagine you saw a production of [public-domain or named play] where the director chose...') because each student writes about their own production. Never reference specific real productions students may not have seen.
drama_content_rules.practitioner_application_per_play: Each set-play unit must include a practitioner-application lesson. Crucible: Brecht for political distance, Stanislavski for Proctor's interior. Blood Brothers: Brechtian narrator, Stanislavski for the leads. Noughts and Crosses: Brechtian distance plus naturalistic intimacy. Around the World in 80 Days: physical theatre, Frantic Assembly, ensemble. Things I Know to Be True: Stanislavski plus Frantic Assembly hybrid (Bovell co-developed with Frantic Assembly). Romeo and Juliet: verse-speaking technique vs heightened style. A Taste of Honey: Theatre Workshop (Joan Littlewood), Brechtian elements (live music, direct address). The Great Wave: documentary theatre and Brechtian witness. The Empress: Brechtian framing of hidden histories with Stanislavskian individual truth.
drama_content_rules.copyright_sensitivity_per_play: Romeo and Juliet is public domain (Shakespeare died 1616). All other 8 plays are in copyright: strict 15-word cap, prefer paraphrase, never reproduce plot. Reference Methuen, Nick Hern and Palgrave editions for context only — never reproduce their editorial notes or page numbers.
drama_content_rules.copyright_drift_grep: Validator hard-bans: 'Award\s+\d+\s+marks\s+for', 'Level [1-9]', 'Component \d', paper codes (8261/W, 8261/C, 8261/X), 'Section A', 'Section B', 'Section C', and verbatim AQA stems. Use StudyVault rubric (Mastering / Secure / Developing / Emerging) for all 8+ mark levels-based mark schemes.
drama_content_rules.glossary_density: Aim for 6 or more inline `<dfn class="term">` glossary entries per lesson. Drama is heavy in stagecraft and practitioner terminology so this is easy to hit; do not pad with non-drama terms.
drama_content_rules.plain_text_rule: Plain unicode in description, practice_questions, knowledge_checks, flashcard_questions, glossary_terms. HTML entities only in *_html fields (content_html, exam_tip_html, conclusion_html).

do_not_use: Level 1 / Level 2 / Level 3 / Level 4 (AQA's tier names)
Award N marks for ... (banned phrasing — validator hard-fail)
Section A / Section B / Section C labels in user-facing strings
Component 1 / Component 2 / Component 3 in user-facing strings
use_instead: 1 mark for X; 1 mark for Y (for short-answer questions)
Up to N marks: ... (for short-answer where multiple credit-worthy points are possible)
Mastering tier (top): describes what the strongest answer shows
Secure tier: describes what a solid answer shows
Developing tier: describes a partial answer
Emerging tier (bottom): describes a minimal answer
studyvault_mark_scheme_rules.performer_designer_lens_required: For 8 marks — Interpret as Performer questions, the mark scheme MUST require both a vocal AND a physical choice anchored to a named moment. For 8 marks — Interpret as Designer questions, the mark scheme MUST require concrete, named design elements (lantern type, gobo, fabric, colour, instrument, soundscape texture) — not generic descriptors like 'dark mood' or 'period costume'.

subject_level_teaching_brief.glossary_target: Six or more glossary terms per lesson, embedded inline as <dfn class="term" data-def="...">. Drama is stagecraft- and practitioner-terminology heavy — proxemics, gestus, gobo, soundscape, blocking, multi-roling, naturalism, fourth wall, tableau — easy to hit; aim for 6–10 per lesson.
subject_level_teaching_brief.flashcard_rules: Eight to fifteen flashcards per lesson. Each answer must be ONE fact, not an enumeration. Bad: 'The four key practitioners are Stanislavski, Brecht, Artaud and Frantic Assembly.' Good: split into four separate cards. Drama-specific card types: term ↔ definition (gestus, gobo, fourth wall), practitioner ↔ technique, play ↔ playwright/year/context, character ↔ defining trait, play ↔ themes.
subject_level_teaching_brief.plain_text_fields_rule: Plain unicode characters only in description, practice_questions[].text/.type/.marks, knowledge_checks[].q, flashcard_questions[].q/.a, glossary_terms[].term/.definition. NEVER HTML entities (’, &, “, —) — these are blocked by the validator. HTML entities are only acceptable inside content_html and other _html-suffixed fields.

unit_level_teaching_brief.synopsis: Phileas Fogg, a precise Victorian gentleman, wagers £20,000 at the Reform Club that he can travel around the world in 80 days. With his French valet Jean Passepartout he sets out from London, pursued by Inspector Fix (who believes Fogg is a bank robber). Across India, Hong Kong, Yokohama, San Francisco and the Atlantic crossing they encounter elephants, typhoons, train robberies and a young Indian widow named Aouda whom they rescue. Eason's stage adaptation distils Verne's 1872 novel into a high-energy ensemble piece for eight actors playing dozens of roles.
major_characters: Phileas Fogg — eccentric Reform Club gentleman; precise, unflappable; the play's still centre
Jean Passepartout — Fogg's French valet; energetic, comic, the audience's emotional way in
Inspector Fix — Scotland Yard detective convinced Fogg is a bank robber
Aouda — young Indian widow rescued from sati; becomes part of Fogg's company
Reform Club gentlemen — the wager-makers in London, framing the adventure
Multi-roled minor parts — train guards, ship's captains, customs officials, brigands, Native American attackers, Yokohama acrobats, an elephant — typically rotated between the small ensemble
major_themes: Time, schedule and Victorian punctuality — the wager itself as a meditation on industrial time
British Empire and the colonial gaze — what Verne sees, what the modern stage chooses to question
Adventure, comedy and the exotic — Victorian thirst for the world reimagined for a modern audience
Friendship and ensemble — Fogg, Passepartout, Aouda, Fix as a found family by the end
The mechanics of travel — steam, rail, the Suez Canal, transcontinental track
Comedy and stoicism — the play laughs with Fogg's eccentricity rather than at the cultures he passes through
unit_level_teaching_brief.historical_context: Verne's novel was published 1872, shortly after the opening of the Suez Canal (1869) and the completion of the US transcontinental railroad (1869) — both made circumnavigation in 80 days theoretically possible for the first time. Eason's stage adaptation premiered at the New Vic Theatre, Newcastle-under-Lyme in 2013 (in-the-round). Modern productions navigate the novel's colonial assumptions by foregrounding the ensemble's awareness of the cultures they pass through.
unit_level_teaching_brief.playwright_context: Jules Verne (1828–1905) — French novelist, founder of speculative adventure fiction. Laura Eason — American playwright (Sex with Strangers; House of Cards writers' room). Her 80 Days adaptation was commissioned by the New Vic and premiered in 2013, dir. Theresa Heskins; designed for a small ensemble (typically 8 actors) with extensive multi-roling and physical-theatre staging.
dramatic_methods: Episodic structure — short scenes in different locations, narrated transitions
Eight-actor ensemble multi-roling — each actor plays many minor parts
Direct address narration — actors step out to set the scene or comment on Fogg's progress
Mime and physical theatre — bodies become trains, ships and elephants
Object transformation — chairs become railway carriages; rope becomes the rigging of a ship
Comic timing — Fogg's stillness against Passepartout's energy
Soundscape-driven scene-setting — train whistles, ship bells, foreign-language fragments
Fast costume changes — base layer plus accessories, like Frantic Assembly / Complicite practice
key_scenes_for_staging: The Reform Club opening — establishing Fogg's precision and the terms of the wager
The Suez Canal customs inspection — Fix's first attempt to detain Fogg
The elephant journey through India — typically staged through ensemble physical theatre
The rescue of Aouda from sati — the play's first real moral stakes
The Hong Kong opium-house scene — Passepartout's misadventure
The crossing of the snowy plains — train under attack by Native American warriors
The Atlantic crossing — burning the deck for fuel
The London ending — apparent failure, then the international-date-line reveal, then the wedding
most_relevant_practitioners: Frantic Assembly — ensemble physical theatre, lifts, bodies-as-objects vocabulary
Complicite — object transformation, storytelling theatre, narrator-led ensemble
Bertolt Brecht — narrator function, episodic structure, songs (some productions interpolate music-hall numbers)
Music-hall and circus traditions — comic precision, audience awareness
unit_level_teaching_brief.copyright_status: in copyright — 15-word cap, paraphrase preferred (Eason adaptation is the prescribed text; Verne novel is public domain but the spec prescribes Eason)
stage_history_highlights: New Vic Newcastle-under-Lyme premiere 2013, dir. Theresa Heskins, in-the-round
common_misconceptions: Students treat the play as a costume drama rather than recognising the ensemble-physical-theatre form Eason is writing for.
Students under-write the role of Aouda and miss her arc from rescued widow to active company member.
Students suggest a literal naturalistic set (a train carriage, an elephant) rather than understanding that the play's pleasure is in transformation by the ensemble.
Students confuse Fogg with a comedic character — examiners reward students who understand his stillness as the comic engine that lets Passepartout's energy land.
Students miss that modern productions actively address Verne's colonial blind spots through performer choice and design — they treat the play as innocent of empire.

“Art is not a mirror held up to reality, but a hammer with which to shape it.” — Bertolt Brecht
“The stage is a magic circle where only the most real things happen.” — Peter Brook
“Theatre is the art of looking at ourselves.” — Augusto Boal
“Stories are how we know ourselves; theatre is how we share that knowing.” — Tanika Gupta
